column3: Its right-and-left spatial grouping offers only a distant directional resonance, not deceptive influence.
Its demand for accountable knowledge provides a framework for testing claims about coercive influence.
Straight speech is a broad corrective to manipulation but does not depict misleading authority.
The right side is a location of recorders here, not a guise of legitimate influence.
It opens the same tribunal by gathering wrongdoers with those bound to their false worship.
Binding agreements made by right hands illuminate the oath-based assurance latent in the focus.
The sexual transgression charge has no relevant link to deceptive leadership or right-side approach.
The leaders immediately deny coercive authority and assign the followers' deviation to their own transgression.
The right hand conveys effective force, a contextual element of the authority the followers allege.
Its retrospective question about earthly duration does not clarify influence or responsibility.
Mutual questioning supplies a structural parallel to the focus's accusatory exchange.
The regulated release of oaths gives limited support to the focus's possible oath-based assurance.
Rejected voluntary or compelled spending is only a broad counterpart to disputed agency.
It continues the same judgment scene by directing the gathered wrongdoers toward Hell.
Taking by the right hand portrays decisive power, one aspect of the alleged authoritative approach.
The condemnation of a separate sexual wrongdoing has no relevant connection.
The tribunal's question about why they do not help one another frames the collapse of their former alliance.
The right side signifies a genuinely blessed and effective standing, contrasting with its false appearance in the focus.
Association with the people of the right gives a contextual contrast between true and claimed right-sided standing.
Universal questioning of creatures supports the focus's later contest over responsibility.
Moses' public claim of messenger authority offers only a general contrast to counterfeit legitimacy.
Right and left describe cosmic directions of prostration, not social influence.
The command to halt them for questioning directly frames the dialogue in which the focus occurs.
Turning away from received signs supports culpability despite warning, though not the leaders' role.
Its blame-laden claim about obedience and death parallels attempts to assign responsibility through speech.
The same scene answers false charges by affirming that the messenger brought truth.
It requires clear authority for a religious claim, directly countering influence dressed as legitimacy.
Alleged partners deny their worshippers' claim at judgment, closely paralleling disavowed responsibility.
A false claim to divine authority is returned to its speaker as punishment, matching the tribunal's claim-testing.
A boast of wealth and status has only a remote connection to the leaders' claimed authority.
Demanding an impossible proof evades clear signs, a related way of resisting legitimate guidance.
The same defendants are shown fully surrendered after their former influence has failed.
Solemn oaths exposed as empty support the focus's possible assurance-based deception.
A claimed covenant is used to reject a messenger, showing authority asserted through an unverified commitment.
The speakers acknowledge that their Lord's sentence has become binding on them in the same exchange.
A companion confronts a false self-assessment with a corrective account of dependence and creation.
The demand for a visible deity shows a people accepting a misleading model of religious authority.
The judgment summons and failed response of invoked partners structurally echo the focus's accountability scene.
Oaths are explicitly turned into a shield for obstructing God's way, a concrete form of legitimacy-based deception.
Right and left are purely geographic features of the cave scene.
It is the immediately preceding mutual-questioning verse that introduces the focus's accusation.
It distinguishes idle oaths from deliberate commitments, clarifying the weight of oath-based assurances.
The idolaters briefly accuse themselves, providing a compact counterpart to contested culpability.
The demand to produce a book invokes textual authority, relevant to the scene's disputed claims of legitimacy.
It defines accountable, binding oaths and therefore supports the focus's weaker oath resonance.
The town asserts a prior prohibition to control Lot's conduct, a limited parallel to coercive social authority.
The demand to report one's answer to messengers extends the judgment's inquiry into responsibility.
The traveler's request for food has no relevant relation to the focus.
Condemned parties blame one another for having brought the punishment upon them, a close reciprocal accusation.
The leaders' immediate reply contests the followers' accusation by denying that they were believers.
It forbids using oaths to block righteous action, linking oath language with obstructive influence.
Dismissing a reforming messenger as bewitched is a related tactic for discrediting legitimate guidance.
Divine aid and victory offer only a broad contrast to the failed authority claimed in the focus.
Emphatic oaths promise belief while the verse exposes their unreliability, closely matching deceptive assurance.
The confession of neglecting prayer does not clarify the leaders' misleading approach.
Mutual speech among the saved is only a distant structural counterpart to the tribunal dialogue.
The dispute over damaging a ship belongs to an unrelated narrative setting.
Calling a messenger bewitched substitutes a discrediting label for engagement with his warning.
The leaders explicitly admit, "We led you astray; we ourselves were astray," the focus's central charge.
The challenge to produce partners gives only a general claim-and-proof resonance.
The question whether Abraham brings truth directly tests a contested claim to legitimate authority.
The promise of divine help is only a broad contrast to the speakers' failed influence.
Moses' request for pardon after forgetting does not concern deceptive leadership.
The rebuke of proud people's gathering and arrogance provides only a general status contrast.
It demands proof for alleged deities, directly challenging authority claims like those underlying the focus.
The introduction to Moses' story has no relevant connection.
Arrogant leaders deny having blocked the weakened from guidance, closely paralleling the focus's leader-follower dispute.
It states that the parties to this dispute will share punishment, resolving their contested responsibility.
Extravagant oaths are rejected in favor of recognizable obedience, exposing assurance without corresponding action.
The condition for receiving a measure of grain has no relevant link.
It concludes the same sequence with God's stated treatment of the criminals.
Kind speech within financial care is a distant ethical contrast, not an account of influence.
The people deflect a reminder by blaming the messengers, a limited accusation parallel.
The apportioned-water narrative does not clarify deceptive authority or responsibility.
Refusal to accept guidance until punishment arrives supports the followers' accountable rejection despite warning.
The people of the right supply a contextual contrast between true right-sided belonging and the focus's claim.
The same people arrogantly reject the declaration of God's sole authority, explaining their culpable response.
Their emphatic oath to follow guidance is exposed by greater aversion when a warner arrives.
The people of the right provide a true eschatological counterpart to the focus's claimed right-side approach.
The description of a heavenly drink has no relevant relation.
A false theological statement shows misuse of speech but not the focus's social influence.
The people of the right form a genuine protected class, contrasting with the focus's deceptive right-side claim.
Provision and resurrection imagery do not clarify the accusatory exchange.
Professed belief without real belief is a close general parallel to a claim of legitimacy masking its absence.
The question about a thief's penalty has no relevant relation.
The same opponents portray the messenger as a mad poet, showing their rejection of legitimate guidance.
Neglecting received signs and then bearing the consequence supports responsibility for rejecting guidance.
The command to defend idols by violence shows coercive communal pressure in defense of false authority.
Noah's enduring descendants do not clarify the focus's dialogue.
The people of the right portray the true ethical content of right-sided standing, contrasting with its false appearance.
Punishment according to what people earned reinforces the focus's rejection of an excuse based on others' influence.
The correction that power belongs to God is a distant contrast to human claims of influential power.
The command to proclaim and turn away gives only a general authority-and-rejection context.
Permitted public complaint by the wronged gives a lawful counterpart to the followers' accusation.
The absence of people restraining corruption offers only a broad social background for collective wrongdoing.
Repeatedly labeling messengers sorcerers or mad discredits truth by attacking its bearer rather than its claim.
The messenger's plain warning is only a broad contrast to misleading influence.
Joseph's explanation of food and personal creed does not illuminate the focus's dispute.
The command to fight in God's way has no relevant link to deceptive leadership.
Truth about Jesus is set against disputed assertions, supporting the focus's contrast between truth and false authority.
Leaders disown those who followed them when punishment becomes visible, directly paralleling the focus's failed leadership bond.
Followers wish they could sever ties with those they followed, extending the focus's mutual blame into irreversible regret.
Satan's intimidation through his allies gives a general model of influence exercised through apparent power.
Turning to false arbiters despite a command to reject them portrays authority that drives people far from the right path.
Those who claim weakness are questioned about their available alternatives, directly qualifying the focus's allocation of responsibility.
Satan openly declares an intention to mislead and command his followers, a general prototype for the alleged influence.
Satan's promises and wishes are explicitly called deception, closely matching influence that arrives with persuasive assurance.
It warns against following people who went astray and led many others astray, directly joining leadership and transmitted error.
A person is pulled into bewilderment while companions call him back to guidance, directly staging rival social influences.
Human and jinn devils ornament false speech for one another, supplying a clear mechanism of plausible-seeming deception.
Following the majority leads away from God's path, a broad counterpart to the followers' misplaced trust in their leaders.
Devils inspire their allies to dispute, showing covert influence exercised through persuasive speech.
Satan declares that he will lie in wait on the straight path to obstruct people, a direct misguiding-agency parallel.
Satan vows to come upon people from their right and left, making this the closest formal parallel to the focus's right-side approach.
Satan whispers a false rationale to Adam and his spouse, exemplifying deception through a plausible religious claim.
Satan swears that he is a sincere adviser, directly matching the focus's weaker resonance of trust won by solemn assurance.
He brings them down through deception after the oath, completing the same pattern of misleading approach and consequence.
The warning not to let Satan tempt people identifies him as an active agent of deceptive removal and exposure.
Later followers accuse earlier communities of leading them astray in the Fire, directly developing intergenerational liability.
Satan makes conduct appear fair, promises support, and then disowns his allies, closely matching deceptive influence followed by withdrawal.
Taking religious authorities as lords gives a broad institutional counterpart to misplaced obedience to human authority.
Religious leaders consume wealth wrongly and obstruct God's path, supplying a concrete form of authority used to mislead.
Manipulating sacred limits is said to lead disbelievers astray while making wrongdoing appear fair.
Moses identifies Pharaoh and his chiefs as an elite whose wealth and display lead people away from God's path.
Pharaoh's command is explicitly called unsound, directly distinguishing apparent rule from legitimate guidance.
Pharaoh leads his people into the Fire, an exact leadership-to-destruction trajectory behind the focus's accusation.
The weak confront the arrogant rulers about following them and ask whether they can relieve any punishment, a close judgment-scene parallel.
Satan denies coercive authority, admits only that he called and they answered, and tells them not to blame him, almost exactly anticipating 37:29-30.
Satan declares that he will make wrongdoing attractive and mislead people, directly describing deceptive influence.
Those who lead others astray bear part of their burdens, directly answering the focus's contested responsibility.
Satan makes prior peoples' deeds appear fair and becomes their patron, a clear model of misleading legitimization.
Satan is authorized to entice those he can with his voice, giving a broad speech-based influence parallel.
Satan is told to mobilize followers through voice, wealth, children, and promises, while his promises are called deception.
Devils are sent to provoke disbelievers, supplying a general account of external incitement.
The Samiri leads Moses' people astray during his absence, a direct human misleader-and-followers parallel.
Satan whispers a promise of immortality and enduring dominion, illustrating influence offered through alluring false assurance.
Following every rebellious devil gives a broad counterpart to choosing a guide who leads away from truth.
Whoever takes Satan as patron is led astray by him and directed toward the Blaze, directly linking allegiance, misguidance, and outcome.
The wrongdoer regrets taking a person as intimate companion on the Day of Judgment, closely paralleling regret over followed influence.
He says that companion led him away from the Reminder after it came to him, an explicit personal account of misguidance.
The companion's leading away from the Reminder is attributed to satanic abandonment, extending the focus's deceptive influence theme.
Taking one's desire as a god gives a broad contrast to submitting judgment to legitimate rather than self-serving authority.
Satan makes a people's deeds fair and bars them from the path while they think otherwise, closely matching misguidance disguised as rightness.
Leaders are made to call toward the Fire and receive no help on Judgment Day, directly paralleling the focus's condemned leaders.
The condemned misleaders say that they led others astray as they themselves went astray, a near verbal and thematic parallel to 37:32.
Disbelievers invite believers to follow their way while falsely offering to bear their sins, a direct case of deceptive assurance and influence.
Those who mislead others bear burdens with their own, directly resolving liability for transmitted error.
It warns against being unsettled by those lacking certainty, a general counterpart to misleading social pressure.
Following inherited practice despite contrary guidance gives a broad model of deferring to an established but misleading authority.
The condemned admit obeying their masters and great ones, who then led them away from the path.
Their plea for doubled punishment for those leaders supplies the judgment consequence of the leadership charge.
The weakened say that, but for the arrogant, they would have believed, directly setting up the same dispute over obstructed guidance.
The weak accuse the arrogant of continual plotting and command to disbelief, explicitly answering the leaders' denial.
The warning not to let worldly life or the deceiver delude people supplies a general deception framework.
Evil deeds are made attractive so that their doer sees them as good, closely explaining the focus's appearance of rightness.
The command not to worship Satan identifies him as an openly misleading authority demanding allegiance.
Satan is said to have led a great multitude astray, directly naming the broad effect of such influence.
It immediately states that the disputants will taste painful punishment, continuing the focus's joint judgment context.
It grounds their recompense in what they used to do, directly qualifying attempts to shift all blame to others.
Satan swears that he will mislead all but God's devoted servants, a direct archetype of deceptive initiative.
The weak in the Fire address the arrogant and ask whether they can bear any share of punishment, closely paralleling follower-leader blame.
The arrogant answer that all are in the Fire and that God has judged between servants, directly denying relief within a shared sentence.
Companions make prior and future conduct appear fair until the sentence falls, closely matching legitimacy-shaped misguidance.
Those who disbelieve seek the people who led them astray in order to punish them more severely, a direct later form of the focus's accusation.
One who turns from the Reminder receives a devil as an intimate companion, establishing a misleading companionship relation.
Those companions bar people from the path while they think themselves guided, directly matching error that arrives as apparent rightness.
At judgment the deceived person curses the companion and recognizes the disastrous bond, closely paralleling the focus's blame exchange.
Satan makes apostasy seem easy and grants false hopes, a general account of persuasive misguidance.
Some promise obedience to those who hate revelation, showing deliberate alliance with an authority opposed to guidance.
Satan makes people forget God's remembrance after taking control of them, a broad counterpart to influence that displaces guidance.
Satan tells a person to disbelieve and then disowns him when he does, closely matching seductive direction followed by abandonment.
Noah says his people followed those whose wealth and children only increased them in loss, directly criticizing deference to social elites.
The leaders are said to have led many astray, an explicit and concise parallel to the focus's accusation.
